title: Private schools to hike tuition next year
summary: Officials of the Coordinating Council of Private Educational Associations and the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines agree that tuition increases are inevitable next school year amid…

blocks.text: November 25, 2026 | 12:00am

At a press conference, COCOPEA chairman Irineo Alvaro Jr. said that like every household, private educational institutions are hit hard by rising inflation, surging electricity and operating costs and frequent calamities.
Pixabay / Tero Vesalainen

MANILA, Philippines — Officials of the Coordinating Council of Private Educational Associations (COCOPEA) and the Catholic Educational Association of the Philippines (CEAP) agree that tuition increases are inevitable next school year amid accelerating inflation.
“These pressures threaten the survival of many schools and make life harder for their students, faculty and staff,” Alvaro said.
Alvaro urged the national government to support policy changes to keep private education sustainable.

“Education agencies should ease strict rules so schools and training institutes can adopt modern, cost-saving and innovative learning modalities without sacrificing quality of education,” Alvaro added.

He said existing tuition fee policies must be reviewed to provide realistic, transparent and timely processes for tuition applications so institutions can sustain fair compensation and support for faculty, invest in modern facilities and continuously improve quality instruction.
“We don’t have other sources, except the support of the government,” Alvaro added.
For his part, Ateneo de Davao University and CEAP president Fr. Karel San Juan said private schools were also affected by the energy crisis amid the war between the United States and Iran.

“If you remember months ago when there was a crisis on energy and fuel because of the war in Iran and the US, all economic forecasts say that it’s going to be a very terrible economy for the Philippines. Our private schools are very sensitive to such economic forecasts because we are really tuition dependent,” San Juan said.
He noted that while the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) asked private schools to suspend tuition fee increases for school year (SY) 2026-2027, some heeded the call of CHED while others did not.

“Why? Because we need to continue running our schools. We need to continue regular across-the-board increases of our faculty and staff. We need to keep pace with the facilities and technological improvements. A simple running of schools will entail increased tuition fees,” San Juan added.
He said the government should allow private schools to decide on tuition fee hikes.

For his part, COCOPEA managing director Joseph Noel Estrada called on CHED and the Department of Education (DepEd) to review the situation. “As my colleagues have said, our tuition guidelines are not only for students but also for faculty and institutions to make them sustainable,” Estrada said.
Education vouchers

Meanwhile, private schools said the enactment of Republic Act 12327 or the Basic Education Voucher Assistance Act is timely as public schools across the country are nearing their breaking point, struggling with packed classrooms, overwhelmed teachers and strained facilities.
Alvaro Jr. said expanding government vouchers to private K-12 schools provides immediate, practical relief by allowing students to move to private basic institutions and decongest public schools.
The law allows students from overcrowded public schools to enroll in private schools using government-funded vouchers.

Signed by the President on Nov. 12, the law will institutionalize a portable, learner-held voucher system, allowing families to choose government-recognized private schools rather than tying subsidies to school-allocated slots under existing programs.
